extracted.intended_audience: public relations practitioners, clients, journalists and general readers interested in PR ethics and reputation
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for public relations firms and practitioners about ethical conduct, client selection, and how actions affect reputation and credibility with clients, professional bodies and the media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Membership and compliance with professional bodies' codes of conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Membership of bodies such as the PRCA (mostly for organisations) and the CIPR (mostly for individual practitioners) signals adherence to codes of conduct and subjects members to disciplinary processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each body has codes of conduct and disciplinary processes and can censure and expel; expulsion is the most serious sanction (PRCA expelled Bell Pottinger and barred rejoining for at least five years). The disciplinary path can include investigation, a provisional ruling and an appeal. Industry professionals hope clients will equate membership with high standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid creating reputational harm through communication
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a critical distinction between helping a client with a bad reputation and creating a bad reputation through the very act of communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners should not adopt strategies that manufacture or deepen reputational damage for third parties; Bell Pottinger’s work is criticised for creating a bad reputation rather than merely defending a client.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not run divisive or racially inflammatory campaigns
rubrics_metrics.description: Campaign messaging must not deliberately or irresponsibly stir up racial or other social tensions (example cited: use of the phrase 'white monopoly capital').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Democratic Alliance accused Bell Pottinger of a 'hateful and divisive campaign to divide South Africa along the lines of race.' Avoiding language and framing that inflames identity-based conflict is an ethical requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful client selection and assessment of reputational risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Taking on controversial or offensive clients is a choice that carries reputational risk for the firm and must be weighed carefully.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The firm did not shy away from controversial clients (examples: FW de Klerk, Asma al-Assad, Oscar Pistorius, the Gupta family). Firms should assess whether representing a client will damage their own or others' reputations; poor choices can lead to client losses and resignations (e.g., HSBC and others reportedly cut ties).

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain the firm's own credibility to be an effective advocate
rubrics_metrics.description: A PR firm's ability to protect or enhance a client's reputation depends on the firm’s own reputation and credibility with journalists and stakeholders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists and other audiences are likely to recall damning incidents; the first response of a journalist contacted by a spokesperson from a discredited firm will be to think of that incident. This makes future lobbying or communications campaigns less convincing when the firm's name is attached.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognise that professional sanctions do not necessarily bar practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Expulsion from a professional association is a serious reputational sanction but does not legally prevent the firm from continuing to operate or to undertake work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Democratic Alliance pointed out Bell Pottinger can still work in South Africa despite expulsion. Distinguish between reputational/industry sanctions and legal/operational ability to practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethics in PR are often voluntary and require accreditation to signal standards
rubrics_metrics.description: In many jurisdictions anyone can call themselves a PR practitioner; ethical standards are therefore promoted through voluntary accreditation and professional membership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author notes that although accredited, there is 'nothing in law' to stop a non-practitioner from claiming PR status. Accreditation and visible adherence to codes are tools to signal higher standards to clients and the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unethical conduct leads to concrete business and organisational consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Unethical or divisive PR activity can result in resignations, loss of clients, expulsion from professional bodies and severe reputational damage that may force structural changes (e.g., firm sale).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The example lists real consequences for Bell Pottinger: the boss resigned, clients walked, the firm was expelled from the PRCA and put itself up for sale. Named clients reportedly ceased using the firm (HSBC and others).
